wizardSteps.title: Your Audience
wizardSteps.description: Who are you trying to reach?

wizardSteps.title: Brand Voice
wizardSteps.description: How do you want to sound?

options.description: Warm and supportive — like a knowledgeable friend who happens to be a coach. Approachable, never pushy.
Direct and punchy — short sentences, no waffle. Confident without being arrogant. Respects the reader's time.
Polished and elevated — positions the coach as a serious expert. Calm confidence. Avoid discounting language.
Plain English only — no jargon, no fitness buzzwords. Anyone could read this and understand it immediately.
Energetic and inspiring — but grounded in real outcomes, not empty hype. Pushes people toward action.

wizardSteps.title: Traffic
wizardSteps.description: Where will your leads come from?

copywriterStyles.name: David Ogilvy
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: Lead with the most important fact or result. Use research and specificity to build credibility: exact numbers, named transformations, precise timelines. Headlines should make a promise rooted in a concrete benefit. Body copy earns the reader's trust through detail, not enthusiasm.

copywriterStyles.name: Gary Halbert
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: Open every piece with a story or personal moment. Write the way smart people talk, not the way companies write. Build emotional connection before you even mention the offer. Use the reader's own frustrations in their own words.

copywriterStyles.name: Eugene Schwartz
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: Never try to create desire — channel the desire that already exists. Match copy to the reader's awareness level. Headlines amplify an existing belief or fear. Use specificity as proof.

copywriterStyles.name: John Caples
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: The headline must appeal to self-interest or arouse intense curiosity. Use the curiosity-gap aggressively. Avoid clever, abstract, or humorous headlines. Body copy should tell a story that leads naturally to the offer.

copywriterStyles.name: Robert Collier
copywriterStyles.tagline: Empathy-first, enter the reader's existing conversation
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: Always enter the conversation already happening in the reader's mind. Open with the reader's current situation before introducing any solution. Use empathy as the primary persuasion mechanism. Build the offer as a natural extension of the reader's own desires.

copywriterStyles.name: Joe Sugarman
copywriterStyles.tagline: The slippery slide — every sentence pulls to the next
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: The only purpose of the headline is to get them to read the first sentence. Keep every sentence short enough that stopping mid-page feels like effort. Open with something surprising, counterintuitive, or confessional. Never resolve a tension — carry it into the next line.

copywriterStyles.name: Dan Kennedy
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: Be blunt. State the problem, state the consequence, state the offer, and close. Deadlines are real — not manufactured. Speak directly to the right person and directly repel the wrong person. Close hard and without apology.

copywriterStyles.name: Bill Bernbach
copywriterStyles.tagline: Witty, disarmingly honest, short punchy lines
copywriterStyles.promptDescription: Honesty is the most powerful persuasion tool. Use wit as a form of respect, not entertainment. Keep sentences short — no sentence should do more than one job. Understatement outperforms hype. Find the one truth about the offer that nobody else will say out loud.
